newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Purge of leftists led to collapse of Albanian army.
newsitem.headline: Purge of leftists led to collapse of Albanian army.

text.p: A purge by Albania's right-wing government of officers with a leftist background contributed to the demoralisation and eventual disintegration of the national army, according to former soldiers.

Two ex-officers, among a crowd of former soldiers waiting outside the defence ministry on Monday to join up again after a call from the new all-party government, spoke with bitterness over what they called the politicisation of the army.

The two, who declined to be named, said after his election in 1992, right-wing President Sali Berisha had ordered a purge of experienced officers belonging to the Communist Party that ruled the tiny Balkan country for over 40 years.
This was a major reason why the army failed to intervene as anti-government rebels looted army barracks of weapons and took control of most of southern Albania last month, they said.

"The professionals were kicked out under the pretext of a reform, and replaced by people who had no clue," a 50-year-old former army captain, sacked for being a former communist, said in an interview.
He said some two-thirds of the officer corps were purged in the mainly conscript army of 40,000, with 150,000 reserves.
"The government totally misunderstood our motivation. We were communists, but we were very patriotic and determined to defend our country," he added.
"They not only purged officers like us, but also senior instructors and professors at military college, many of them trained in the Soviet Union," he added.

He was scathing about the defence minister in the rightist government that resigned earlier this month, Safet Zhulali, a former provincial schoolteacher from Berisha's Democratic Party who fled to Italy last week in the midst of the crisis.
"He betrayed us and the country, leaving the army in disarray," he said. "If the captain leaves his ship, it will run aground."

Early in March, after the first barracks were looted in the south, the former minister dismissed army chief General Sheme Kosova for failing to ensure adequate security against the "terrorists", who were accused of being backed by the left.
The talk in the street was that Kosova was sacked for refusing to order his soldiers to fire on Albanian civilians.
Another ex-officer, a 32-year-old former lieutenant, said he had quit the army in disgust over the incompetence of senior officers, their treatment of juniors and low pay.

"We were treated just like the ordinary soldiers, eating the same food, mainly tea and spaghetti," said the former officer, who studied for eight years at military college and earned around $80 a month in the army.

He said another reason for the collapse of morale in the army, particularly in the more prosperous south, was anger over money which thousands of families lost in failed savings schemes the government allowed to flourish.
He said he wanted to sign up again partly because he needed a job, but also because he felt the country needed him and his experience.

Both men were full of praise for new Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj of the main opposition Socialists, heirs to the communists, saying: "He doesn't care whether people are from the left or the right, he just wants to build an army like the one we had before -- small, but able to defend the country."
"We need to take politics out of the army," he added.
